question_types.statement: (3.1) Solve one (at your choice) among Exercises (2.1)-(2.2)-(2.3) using z3.

(2.3) Apply CDCL (IDL) to determine whether the following set of clauses
is satisﬁable or not:
x1−x2≤− 5, x 2−x3≤ 0, (x1≤ 0)∨(x3 < 16), (x1 > 1)∨(x3−x1≤ 3) .
[Hint: solving this exercise by hand may require some time and patience,
solve ﬁrst some easy exercise in the next group, e.g. from (3.1).]
Part III: Exercises to be solved with z3.

(2.1) Check whether the set of clauses below is satisfiable or not:
¬p1 ∨ p3 ∨ p4 p1 ∨ p2 p1 ∨ p3
p1 ∨ ¬p2 ∨ ¬p4 ¬p1 ∨ ¬p4
via ordered resolution or CDCL (do not use truth tables).

(1.4) Explain the refutational completeness theorem for propositional reso-
lution.
Part II: Exercises to be solved manually.

(1.2) Transform the following sentence into prenex normal form and Skole-
mize it:
∃x (¬∃y∃z (h(x, y, z) = h(x, z, y)) → ∀y (x = y)) .

(3.2) Human observers in an exclusive club on Ganymede can’t distinguish
Martians from Venusians, males from females, except for the fact that Venu-
sian women and Martian men always tell the truth and Venusian men and
Martian women always lie. A says ”I’m from Mars”; B exclaims ”That’s not
true!”. A and B have different sex (they are even married); are they a mixed
couple (i.e. is one of them from Mars and the other one from Venus)?
(1.2) Formulate the T -Propagation Rule of the CDCL (T )-procedure.

(1.2) Skolemize the following sentence:
∃y ∀x ∃z (P (f (x, y)) → x = f (z, z) ∨ y = f (z, z)) .

(2.3) Apply congruence closure to the following set of literals
f (a, b) = g(c), b = g(c), f (a, c) ̸= a, g (b) = a, c = b
and check whether it is satisfiable or not.
Part III: Exercises to be solved with z3.

(2.1) Determine whether the following formula is a tautology or not (negate
it, bring it to conjunctive normal form and apply CDCL):
(p → ((q → r) → r)) → (p → (q ∨ r))

(1.2) Which one among the following formulae is in negation normal form
(NNF)?
¬(p ∧ q), p ∧ ¬(¬q ∨ ¬r), (p ∨ q) ∨ ¬q
Bring to NNF the above formulae which are not in NNF.

(2.1) Compute a conjunctive normal form for the following formula:
¬(p → ¬r) ∨ (r → ¬q) ∨ ¬(¬q → p) .

(2.2) Determine whether the following inference is correct or not
Some trains are fast and some are not.
Regional trains are not fast.
There are non-regional fast trains.
using Skolemization, Herbrand Theorem and Ground Resolution.

(1.3) Which one among the following algorithms requires ‘large’ space re-
sources consumption?
(a) Quantiﬁer-free satisﬁability in IDL; (b) Resolution; (c) Congruence Closure.
Part II: Exercises to be solved manually.

(1.4) Explain why propositional resolution is efficient when applied to sets
of Horn clauses.
Part II: Exercises to be solved manually.

(1.2) Write down a formula of L containing both a free and a bound occur-
rence of the variable x.

(3.3) You are given the following 10 tiles: 1 | 3 , 6 | 1 , 3 | 2 , 9 | 6 ,
1 | 2 , 4 | 9 , 2 | 6 , 2 | 4 , 6 | 1 , 2 | 2 . Each tile has two cells,
with numbers printed inside them. Arrange the tiles in a square frame in such
a way that two adjacent cells from diﬀerent tiles have the same number (or
show that no such arrangement exists).[Hint: use the declare-datatypes
utility to declare the 10-members set comprising your tiles. Then introduce
two Int-valued functions representing the content of the left and the right
cells. Use a further Int-valued function to formalize the position (from 1 to
10) of each tile in the solution frame.]

(1.1) Suppose we are given a language L consisting of a ternary predicate
D, a binary predicate R, a unary predicate P and three individual constants
a, b, c.
• What are the variables occurring free in the following formula?
∃y∀x (D(x, y, x)→ P (y))→ R(x, z)
• Write down the ground instances of the universal formula
∀x (D(a, b, c)→ P (x)∨ R(x, x)) .
• Skolemize the sentence
∃y∃x (D(x, y, x)∨ P (y)).

(2.2) Determine whether the following inference is correct or not
Mary visited only warm countries.
African countries are warm countries
Mary visited all African countries.
using Skolemization, Herbrand Theorem and ground Resolution.

(1.3) Formulate the statement of the refutational completeness theorem of
the propositional Resolution calculus.

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a binary predicate symbol R, a
binary function simbol f and individual constants a, b. The identity predicate
also belongs to L.
• Write down a ground term and a non-ground term in L.
• Which one among the following clauses contains both a ground and a
non ground literal?
R(a, x) ∨ a ̸= b, ¬R(f (a, b), b) ∨ f (a, a) = b, a = x ∨ a = f (x, x).

(2.3) Check whether the following set of clauses is consistent or not
f (g(x), y) ̸= z g (x) = y ∨ g(y) = y, f (y, y) = z, g (x) = g(y),
using CDCL modulo EUF.
Part III: Exercises to be solved with z3.

(2.1) Check the consistency of the following set of clauses
p ∨ ¬q, ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r, q ∨ r,
q ∨ ¬r, ¬r ∨ s, ¬s ∨ ¬r ∨ ¬q
using the CDCL procedure.

(1.3) Which one(s) among the following clauses are not Horn clauses?
a = b, R (x, a) ∨ R(y, b), x = y ∨ R(y, x), ¬R(x, y) .

(2.1) Check that the following formula is a tautology
(p → (q ∧ r)) → (p → q) ∧ (p → r) .

(3.3) The game board below
    
      +---+---+---+
      | 4 | 1 | 3 |
      +---+---+---+
      | 2 | 5 |   |
      +---+---+---+
      
has blocks with numbers in it. Also there is a single ”hole” that can be used
for moving the blocks: a block can be swapped with the ”hole” only if it is
in the same row or column as the ”hole”. Move the blocks so as to have the
blocks numbered 1,2,3 on the first row and the blocks numbered 4,5 followed
by the ”hole” on the second row. How many moves do you need at least?

(1.1) Suppose we are given a language L consisting of a ternary predicate D,
a binary predicate R, a unary function symbol f and the individual constants
a, b. The identity predicate also belongs to L.
• Write down 3 diﬀerent ground atomic sentences of L.
• Which one among the following formulae is a universal sentence (recall
that a sentence is a formula without free variables)?
∃x ∀y D(y, a, x), ∀x (R(y, x) → f(x) = b), ∀x (f(x) = x ∨ R(a, b))

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a ternary predicate symbol S, a
binary function simbol g, a unary function symbol f and individual constants
a, b, c. The identity predicate also belongs to L.
• Write down an positive groundL-literal and a negative groundL-literal.
• Which one among the following expressions are L-formulae (carefully
take in mind the arities assigned above)?
¬S(a, x, a), ∃x S(x),
g(a) = c, S (x, g(x, x), g(y, y)).

(3.2) The police detained four suspects: Alice, Bruno, Carlo and Davide,
at least one of whom is certainly guilty of theft. The four, when questioned,
make the following statements. Alice and Carlo say that only one in the
group is guilty, Bruno says that Alice and Davide are both guilty, while
Davide says that Alice is guilty. Knowing that at most one of them is lying
and that the others are telling the truth, who is/are guilty?

(3.2) A very special island is inhabited only by knights and knaves. Knights
always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. You meet four inhabitants: Bart,
Dave, Rex and Zoey. Bart tells you that Rex and Dave are both knights or
both knaves. Dave tells you that Zoey is a knave. Rex claims, “Bart is
a knave.” Zoey claims, “Rex is a knight and Dave is a knave.” Can you
determine who is a knight and who is a knave?

(3.3) I have to transport (from one side of a river to the other) 40 sacks of
flour weighing 4 weight units each, 25 sacks of flour weighing 3 weight units
each and 20 sacks of flour weighing 1 weight unit each; my boat can carry
a maximum of 50 weight units. How many crossings do I have to make,
considering that my own additional weight is 12 weight unit?

(3.2) What is the minimum number of colors needed to color the portion
of the Middle East Country map including exactly the following countries:
Turkey, Syria, Jordan, Iran, Iraq, Kuweit, Saudi Arabia? (A picture of the
Middle East Country map is available for downloading at yout terminal).

(3.3) The diagram below shows a cross-shaped box containing three numbe-
red blocks.
Slide the blocks around the box until the numbers read 1, 2, 3 as you go
horizontally from left to right. How do you do it? And how many moves
does it take?

(1.1) List the unary predicates, the binary predicates, the unary functions
symbols and the binary functions symbols occurring in the formula
∀x(P (f (g(x, z)), y) ∧ Q(f (a), x) → S(y)) .

(1.3) Which one(s) among the following literals are flat?
f (x) = f (y), ¬x = y, ¬f (x) = f (z), f (x) = x

(3.2) How many colors are needed to color the South America country map?
Are three colors sufficient?

(2.2) Determine whether the following inference is correct or not
There are friends of yours that are not friends of mine.
All friends of mine like skiing.
Some friends of yours do not like skiing.
using Skolemization, Herbrand Theorem and Ground Resolution.

(2.2) Determine whether the following inference is correct or not
Some customers of ours are demanding.
Demanding people are never satisfied.
John is satisfied.
John is not our customer.
using Skolemization, Herbrand Theorem and Ground Resolution.

(2.2) Determine whether the following inference is correct or not
Some people are careful and some other are not.
Careful people do not make mistakes.
Some people make mistakes.
using Skolemization, Herbrand Theorem and Ground Resolution.

(2.2) Determine whether the following inference is correct or not
All cats are felines.
All felines have whiskers.
If Tom doesn ’t have whiskers he is not a cat.
using Skolemization, Herbrand Theorem and Ground Resolution.

(1.2) Put the following sentence in prenex normal form and skolemize it:
∃y (∃xR(x, y) → ∀x(g(f (x), y) = x) ∨ R(a, b)) .

(1.4) Illustrate ordered resolution rule.
Part II: Exercises to be solved manually.

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a binary predicate symbol R,
a unary function simbol f and individual constants a, b, c. The identity
predicate also belongs to L.
• Write down an L-sentence containing at least an existential quantifier.
• Which one among the following L-formulae is a ground clause?
¬R(a, a) ∨ x = y, (a = c ∧ a = b) ∨ ¬R(a, c),
P (x, y) ∨ x = b ∨ f (a) = c, f (b) = b ∨ R(c, f(c)).

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a ternary predicate symbol R
and individual constants a, b, c. The identity predicate also belongs to L.
• Write down a ground Horn non-unit clause in L (recall that ‘non-unit’
means ‘with more than one literal’).
• Which one(s) among the following formulae are universal sentences?
¬∀x R(x, a, x), ∀x(x = a ∨ y = b), ∀x ∀z(R(a, x, z) → R(x, z, z)).

(1.3) Suppose we order the propositional variables as p < q < r < s. In order
to saturate the following set of clauses
p ∨ q, ¬q ∨ ¬r, ¬q ∨ s
do we need 0,1 or 2 ordered resolution steps? Why?

(1.4) Give the definition of a Horn clause; supply an example of a Horn
clause and of a clause which is not Horn.
Part II: Exercises to be solved manually.

(1.3) Write down an L-formula which is in NNF (negation normal form) but
not in CNF (conjunctive normal form).

(3.3) Use z3 to find the path in the following labyrinth from the entry point
(marked ⇓) to the exit point (marked ⇐).
✠ ✠ ⇓
✠ ✠
✠ ✠ ✠ ✠
✠ ✠ ✠
✠ ✠ ✠ ✠
✠ ✠ ✠
✠ ✠ ✠
⇐ ✠ ✠
[Hint: use a bounded model-checking technique. Represent the coordinates
of the current position (in a 8 × 8 grid) by a couple of integer variables
x, y. Each move in the transition system increments or decrements one of
the two variables (take care of the fact that cases marked with✠ cannot be
occupied!).]

(2.3) Check whether the following set of atoms is consistent or not in real
arithmetics using Fourier-Motzkin:
(x < z), x + y + z >0, (y <0), (x + z) < y .
Part III: Exercises to be solved with z3.

(3.3) You can move yourself inside the grid below in two ways: (i) you can
occupy an adjacent 1 cell provided the latter is empty; (ii) you can push
forward an adjacent obstacle ✠ to the cell adjacent to it (provided such a
cell is empty) and occupy the position of the obstacle. You want to move
from the left upper corner to the right lower corner: is it possible? how many
moves do you need?
→ ✠ ✠
✠ ✠
✠

[Hint: use a bounded model checking technique. This is a possible formali-
zation: use an integer variable to denote your current position and an array
a of Booleans to represent the status of the grid (where(select a i) is
equal to true if and only if the celli is occupied by an obstacle. It could
be useful to add an extra variable whose role is that of indicating the cell
adjacent to the obstacle in case of a move of the kind (ii) - in case of a move

to take any value. ]

(3.3) Start with a bag with 10 white balls and 9 black balls. Take out two
balls: if they have the same color, put a black ball into the bag; if they have
a different color, put a white ball back into the bag. Show that last ball left
cannot be white. [Hint: use a transition system with two integer variables
counting the current number of black and white balls in the bag.]

(3.3) Prove that among ﬁve persons we meet at a party, it might in principle
happen that three of them are familiar with each other and three of them
are not familiar with each other (of course the two groups won’t be disjoint).
[Hint: use the declare-datatypes utility to declare a 5-members set,
representing the set of the persons we met at the party; then introduce the
‘familiarity’ binary relation on it. The only property concerning the familia-
rity relation you need to take into account is that it is a symmetric relation,
namely that “for all x and y, if x is familiar with y, then y is familiar with
x”. You should check that the above described situation is consistent.]

(3.3) Prove that we can always choose 3 diﬀerent persons who are either
familiar with each other or not familiar with each other, from 6 persons we
meet at a party. [Hint: use the declare-datatypes utility to declare a
6-members set, representing the set of the persons we met at the party; then
introduce the ‘familiarity’ binary relation on it. The only property concerning
the familiarity relation you need to take into account is that it is a symmetric
relation, namely that “for all x and y, if x is familiar with y, then y is familiar
with x”. Prove unsatisﬁability of a situation where there are not 3 mutually
familiar and 3 mutually unfamiliar persons.]

(3.3) Show that the proposed solution of the detective story below is correct:
Someone who lives in Dreadbury Mansion killed Aunt Agatha. Agatha, the
butler, and Charles live in Dreadbury Mansion, and are the only people who
live therein. A killer always hates his victim, and is never richer than his
victim. Charles hates no one that Aunt Agatha hates. Agatha hates everyone
except the butler. The butler hates everyone not richer than Aunt Agatha.
The butler hates everyone Aunt Agatha hates. No one hates everyone. Aga-
tha, Charles and the butler are different persons. Therefore: Agatha killed
herself.
[Hint: you do not need to impose specific constraints on the word “richer”,
just treat it as a free binary predicate symbol.]

(3.2) Our Italian region Lombardia has 12 provinces: Varese (Va), Lecco
(Le), Como (Co), Sondrio (So), Monza-Brianza (MB), Milano (Mi), Bergamo
(Be), Brescia (Br), Pavia (Pa), Lodi (Lo), Cremona (Cr), Mantova (Ma).
The border relations are: (Va-Co), (Va-Mi), (Va-MB), (Co-Le), (Co-So),
(Co-MB), (Le-So), (Le-Be), (Le-MB), (So-Be), (So-Br), (MB-Be), (MB-Mi),
(Be-Br), (Be-Cr), (Be-Mi), (Br-Cr), (Br-Ma), (Mi-Pa), (Mi-Lo), (Mi-Cr),
(Pa-Lo), (Lo-Cr), (Cr-Ma).
Find the minimum number of colors needed to color this geographic map.

(3.3) Find a solution for the following tetravex game
[Hint: tiles need not be rotated, but they should be placed in such a way that
left-right and top-down colors match. Introduce an enumerated datatype for-
med by the 9 tiles and an enumerated datatype formed by the colors you see in
the picture; use also Int-valued functions for horizontal, vertical coordinates
in the solution, as well as for top, bottom, left, right colors of each tile.]

(3.2) The Italian region Toscana has 10 provinces: Massa-Carrara (MC),
Lucca (Lu), Pistoia (P), Prato (Pr), Firenze (Fi), Arezzo (Ar), Livorno (Li),
Pisa (Pi), Siena (Si), Grosseto (Gr).
The border relations are: (MC-Lu), (Lu-P), (Lu-Pi), (P-Pr), (P-Fi), (Pr-
Fi), (Fi-Pi), (Fi-Si), (Fi-Ar), (Li-Pi), (Li-Gr), (Pi-Si), (Pi-Gr), (Si-Ar), (Si-
Gr).
Find the minimum number of colors needed to color this geographic map.

(3.2) A very special island is inhabited only by knights and knaves. Knights
always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. You meet four inhabitants: Bart,
Marge, Zed and Rex. Bart tells you that Zed is a knight or Rex is a knight.
Marge tells you that Zed and Bart are both knights. Zed says, “I and Rex
are knights.” Rex tells you that Zed is a knave.
Can you determine who is a knight and who is a knave?

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising binary predicate symbols R, S
and individual constants a, b, c. The identity predicate also belongs to L.
• Write down a ground L-atom whose root symbol is the identity pre-
dicate and a ground L-atom whose root symbol is not the identity
predicate.
• Which one(s) among the following expressions are L-formulae?
¬S(a, x, a), ∃x S(x, a),
a = b, R (c) .

(3.2) Someone has been secretly eating the butcher’s sausages! The four bad
boys suspected of the misdeed stated the following:
-Andrea : Beatrice ate the sausages!
-Beatrice : Davide ate them all!
-Carlo : I certainly didn’t eat them!
-Davide : Beatrice is definitely lying!
Only one of them is telling the truth. The other three are obviously lying.
Can you tell who ate the sausages?

(3.2) A very special island is inhabited only by knights and knaves. Knights
always tell the truth, and knaves always lie.
You meet three inhabitants: Zoey, Peggy and Mel. Zoey says that it’s
not the case that Mel is a knave. Peggy tells you that Mel and Zoey are both
knights. Mel says that Zoey is a knight or Peggy is a knave.
Can you determine who is a knight and who is a knave?

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a unary predicate symbol P , a
unary function simbol f and individual constants a, b. The identity predicate
also belongs to L.
• Write down a ground negative literal and a non-ground negative literal
in L.
• Which one(s) among the following formulae are sentences?
¬P (b)∨¬f (a) = b, ¬∀x (P (x) → f (x) = x), ¬∃x (f (y) = x∧¬P (x)).

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a binary predicate symbol R, a
binary function simbol f and individual constants a, b. The identity predicate
also belongs to L.
• Write down a ground literal and a non-ground literal in L.
• Which one among the following atomic formulae contains both a ground
and a non ground term?
R(a, f(b, b)), R (a, x), a = b, R (x, f(x, y)).

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a binary predicate R, a unary
function simbol f and individual constants a, b, c. The identity predicate also
belongs to L.
• Write down a ground atomic formula and a non-ground atomic formula
of L.
• Which one among the following expressions are formulae of L?
f (x), R (x, f(x)), ∃x (x = b), f (f (c)).

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a binary predicate symbol R, a
unary function simbol g and individual constants a, b. The identity predicate
also belongs to L.
• Write down a positive ground literal and a negative ground literal of
the language L.
• Which one among the following expressions are terms of L?
g(g(a)), R (a, a), a = b, x.

(1.1) Suppose we are given a language L consisting of a ternary predicate D,
a unary predicate P and one individual constant a.
• What are the ground atomic formulae that can be written in this
language?
• Which ones among the following sentences are in prenex normal form?
∀y (D(y, a, a) → P (y)), ∀x (P (x) → ∃y D(x, x, y)), ∀x ∃y ∀z D(x, y, z)

(3.2) A greengrocer can put in his bag Apples, Oranges, Bananas, Melons.
The weights of each of these items are 0.25, 0.3, 0.15, 0.4 Kg, respectively.
He plans to sell such items earning $ 4, $ 5, $ 3, $ 7, for each of such items,
respectively. Knowing that its bag capacity is 13 Kg, check whether it is
possible for him to earn $ 260 (or more).

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a unary predicate P , a binary
function simbol f and individual constants a, b. The identity predicate also
belongs to L.
• Write down a ground term and a non-ground term of L.
• Which one among the following expressions are sentences of L?
P (f (a, x)), ∀x P(f (a, x)), ∃x (x = b), ∃x (x = y).

(1.1) We are given a language L comprising a ternary function symbol h and
individual constants a, b, c. The identity predicate also belongs to L.
• Write down a ground negative literal in L.
• Which one(s) among the following formulae are universal sentences?
∀x (a = b → h(a, a, x) = h(a, a, y)), ¬∀x h(a, a, x) ̸= b, ∀x (x = a).

(3.2) A very special island is inhabited only by knights and knaves. Knights
always tell the truth, and knaves always lie. You meet two inhabitants: Zed
and Alice. Zed tells you, “I am a knight or Alice is a knave.” Alice tells you,
“Of Zed and I, exactly one is a knight.” Can you determine who is a knight
and who is a knave?

(1.3) Consider a universal sentence like ∀x (h(x, x, x) ̸= x): which one of the
following statements is correct?
(a) The sentence has three ground instances in the language L.
(b) The sentence does not have any ground instance in the language L.
(c) The sentence has infinitely many ground instances in the language L.

(3.2) I need to buy marker pens and I can spend at most $ 100. They sell:
small boxes (containing 5 items) for $ 3, medium boxes (containing 10 items)
for $ 5 and big boxes (containing 20 items) for $ 8. Check that 245 is the
maximum number of marker pens I can buy.

(3.3) Each customer in a pizzeria got a different pizza; taking into conside-
ration the information from the picture below, can you determine who got
the one with capers and olives?

(1.3) Consider the universal sentence ∀x∀yR(x, y, a): how many ground
instances does it have in the language L?

(1.1) Suppose we are given a languageL consisting of a ternary predicate D,
a binary predicate R, a unary predicate P and two individual constants a, b.
• What are the variables occurring free in the following formula?
∀z∃y (D(z, y, x)→ P (y))∨ R(z, z)
• Write down the ground instances of the universal formula
∀x∀y(D(a, b, b)→ P (x)∨ R(x, y)) .
• Skolemize the sentence
∀y∃z (D(y, y, z)→ P (z)).

(2.2) Determine whether the following inference is correct or not
Cars are not allowed to circulate here, unless they have an electric engine.
